In the humanities, fields such as English and history often centre on work by individual scholars, including single-authored articles and monographs. title: Profile of the SMU-affiliated research corpus
text:
Section Summary
The SMU-affiliated research corpus spans 148 Web of Science subject categories. Astronomy and astrophysics has the most publications among the fields matched to SMU academic units, while business and economics has the widest range of publication venues. Canadian journals are the most common venues in several fields, including geology, chemistry, and history. Annual publication output grew by 5.7%, and 63% of publications appeared in the most recent 15 years. The median publication received eight citations. A chemistry paper on ionic liquids leads in total citations, while astronomy collaborations occupy the top three places by average annual citations. International co-authorship accounts for 41.2% of the corpus, and 22% of publications have a sole author. This range of authorship practices helps explain why rankings by publication count shift when each publication is divided among its authors. Standard articles make up about three-quarters of the records in the document-type summary, with conference contributions, book reviews, and monograph chapters among the other forms of scholarship represented.
I read the Web of Science corpus as showing two concentrations of publication activity at SMU. One is in the physical and earth sciences. Astronomy and astrophysics leads the matched subject categories with 1,033 publications, and chemistry (593), geology (450), and physics (434) each contribute substantial bodies of work. The other is in business and economics, which approaches astronomy in publication volume (924) and spans the widest range of venues (369). Psychology, with 585 publications, is another centre of activity, close to chemistry in volume. The citation rankings add a different dimension to this profile. Astronomy collaborations occupy the first three positions by average annual citations, while a chemistry paper leads in total citations and work on corporate environmental strategy appears in both rankings.
I interpret these patterns in light of what Web of Science indexes. The publication counts depend on which journals, books, and conference proceedings the database covers, and the citation counts depend on which citations it captures. This point is relevant because fields communicate their research through different outlets. A field that publishes principally in indexed journals may be more visible in this profile than one in which monographs, book chapters, or locally oriented venues play a larger role. I therefore take these concentrations as an account of where SMU’s research is most visible in Web of Science, with the same coverage in mind when interpreting which work has drawn the most citations.

title: Chemistry
text:
Cluster 7 brings together research on how compounds are made, how their atoms are arranged, and how that arrangement shapes their behaviour. Several communities focus on metal complexes, in which groups called ligands bind to a metal centre. Some examine how these complexes are built or how they come apart. Others ask how changes to the ligands affect the reactions a complex can take part in. X-ray methods, spectroscopy, and computer calculations recur across these communities as ways to determine molecular structure and explain chemical behaviour.
The study of reactivity connects this work to questions about how to make particular products. Some communities examine how catalysts help join molecules into polymer chains or form bonds between carbon and nitrogen. Others look at how compounds gain or lose electrons, including work on indium and bismuth that extends the cluster’s scope beyond transition metals. The interest in structure also extends to arrangements involving many molecules, as in studies of hydrogen-bond networks in solids and salts that can remain liquid near room temperature.
Several communities give this chemistry a materials or biomedical application. Research on atomic layer deposition evaluates metal compounds as starting materials for growing thin films. The biomedical communities ask different questions about what compounds do in living systems, from their potential activity against tuberculosis to the role of cholinesterase enzymes in Alzheimer’s research and the toxicity of compounds following exposure.
Renewable energy design forms a distinct engineering strand within the cluster. Its focus is on how generation, storage, and control can be combined to meet goals such as lower cost or to support an application such as desalination. The unit of design here is an operating system, while much of the chemistry research asks how the properties of individual compounds can be understood and put to use.
Three forms of evidence below show what the keyword communities are about and how they relate to one another.
Interactive keyword network. Each point represents a keyword, and a line connects two keywords that appear together in one or more publications. The full network shows how keyword communities relate to one another. Select a community from the dropdown to see which terms group together and which connect to terms in other communities. Connections within a community show which subjects, methods, or concepts appear together. Connections across communities show where their vocabularies overlap.
Community word clouds. Each cloud shows the vocabulary of one community. Larger words have higher within-community PageRank. This measure reflects both the strength of a keyword’s connections and how well connected its neighbours are. Larger words therefore show which terms are most prominent in the community’s pattern of connections. Smaller words can give those terms context by identifying particular subjects, settings, or methods.
Affiliated publications. Each publication has a set of membership values, one for each community. A value of 1 means that all of the publication’s keyword-based membership is assigned to that community. When membership is distributed across communities, the values show how that affiliation is shared. For example, values of 0.7 and 0.3 indicate that the publication’s keywords align more strongly with the first community while also connecting it to the second. The publication lists show how the themes visible in the keyword network are represented in the institution’s research.

















Community 1 of Cluster 7 centres on how metal complexes are put together and how they react. “Complexes” (0.077), “chemistry” (0.075), “reactivity” (0.060), and “derivatives” (0.054) have the highest within-community PageRank. The structural terms give this focus more detail. “Crystal-structures,” “structural-characterization,” and “ligand” point to questions about how atoms and ligands are arranged around metals such as osmium and tungsten. “Activation,” “insertion,” “oxidative addition,” and “reductive elimination” point to how bonds break, form, or rearrange during reactions. Catalysis is one part of that broader inquiry, with hydroboration among the transformations under study. The table also points to work on boron dyes. For comparisons with the communities that follow, the defining feature here is the attention given to both the structure of metal complexes and the changes they undergo.












Community 2 of Cluster 7 centres on how researchers determine and explain the structure of crystals and molecules. “Crystal-structure” has the highest within-community PageRank (0.084), followed by “molecular-structure” (0.042) and “ab initio” (0.035). Diffraction, Raman spectroscopy, and carbon-13 NMR point to different kinds of experimental evidence, while “ab initio” and “basis-sets” point to calculations used to model molecular structures and interpret their properties. Keywords such as “symmetry” and “vibrational spectrum” show the kinds of features this work seeks to explain. “Restricted rotation” and “fluxional properties” add a question about how molecular arrangements change, while “hydration,” “dehydration,” and “aqua complexes” point to an interest in how compounds incorporate, bind, or lose water.
Ligands and metal complexes connect this community to Community 1. Both examine how atoms are arranged around metal centres, with examples here involving chromium, copper, and iron. Community 1 connects those arrangements to reactions such as insertion and oxidative addition. Community 2 gives more weight to the methods used to establish molecular structure and to questions about how that structure varies with molecular motion or interaction with water.












Community 3 of Cluster 7 centres on how renewable energy systems are designed and operated. “Design” has the highest within-community PageRank (0.139), followed by “optimization” (0.038). “Generation,” “storage,” “energy management,” and “control” point to two related questions: which components to combine, and how to coordinate them once the system is operating. “Cost” identifies a criterion for evaluating design choices, while “desalination” gives the work a specific application.
The distinction from Communities 1 and 2 is the scale of the research. Community 1 examines the structure and reactivity of metal complexes, and Community 2 examines how researchers determine crystal and molecular structure. Community 3 shifts the focus to how technologies are configured and managed to meet an operating goal, giving the cluster a distinct engineering strand.












This community brings compound discovery and characterization into a biomedical setting, with tuberculosis as the named application. “Aliphatic amines” identifies a class of compounds, while “lipophilic” points to an interest in how readily compounds associate with fats or other nonpolar environments. “Discovery” and “antimicrobial” give those terms a biological context. “Copper,” “manganese,” and “crystal” also point to work on metal compounds and their structures, though the keyword table leaves open how closely that work relates to the tuberculosis research.
The metal and crystal terms connect this community to Communities 1 and 2, which examine the structure and reactivity of metal complexes and the methods used to determine molecular structure. What stands out here is the question of what compounds might do in a biological setting, particularly their potential antimicrobial activity.

title: Chemistry
text: Community 1 of Cluster 7 centres on how metal complexes are put together and how they react. “Complexes” (0.077), “chemistry” (0.075), “reactivity” (0.060), and “derivatives” (0.054) have the highest within-community PageRank. The structural terms give this focus more detail. “Crystal-structures,” “structural-characterization,” and “ligand” point to questions about how atoms and ligands are arranged around metals such as osmium and tungsten. “Activation,” “insertion,” “oxidative addition,” and “reductive elimination” point to how bonds break, form, or rearrange during reactions. Catalysis is one part of that broader inquiry, with hydroboration among the transformations under study. The table also points to work on boron dyes. For comparisons with the communities that follow, the defining feature here is the attention given to both the structure of metal complexes and the changes they undergo.

title: Chemistry
text:
Community 2 of Cluster 7 centres on how researchers determine and explain the structure of crystals and molecules. “Crystal-structure” has the highest within-community PageRank (0.084), followed by “molecular-structure” (0.042) and “ab initio” (0.035). Diffraction, Raman spectroscopy, and carbon-13 NMR point to different kinds of experimental evidence, while “ab initio” and “basis-sets” point to calculations used to model molecular structures and interpret their properties. Keywords such as “symmetry” and “vibrational spectrum” show the kinds of features this work seeks to explain. “Restricted rotation” and “fluxional properties” add a question about how molecular arrangements change, while “hydration,” “dehydration,” and “aqua complexes” point to an interest in how compounds incorporate, bind, or lose water.
Ligands and metal complexes connect this community to Community 1. Both examine how atoms are arranged around metal centres, with examples here involving chromium, copper, and iron. Community 1 connects those arrangements to reactions such as insertion and oxidative addition. Community 2 gives more weight to the methods used to establish molecular structure and to questions about how that structure varies with molecular motion or interaction with water.

Community 3 of Cluster 7 centres on how renewable energy systems are designed and operated. “Design” has the highest within-community PageRank (0.139), followed by “optimization” (0.038). “Generation,” “storage,” “energy management,” and “control” point to two related questions: which components to combine, and how to coordinate them once the system is operating. “Cost” identifies a criterion for evaluating design choices, while “desalination” gives the work a specific application.
The distinction from Communities 1 and 2 is the scale of the research. Community 1 examines the structure and reactivity of metal complexes, and Community 2 examines how researchers determine crystal and molecular structure. Community 3 shifts the focus to how technologies are configured and managed to meet an operating goal, giving the cluster a distinct engineering strand.

The metal and crystal terms connect this community to Communities 1 and 2, which examine the structure and reactivity of metal complexes and the methods used to determine molecular structure. What stands out here is the question of what compounds might do in a biological setting, particularly their potential antimicrobial activity.

text: This community focuses on how chemical species bind to form adducts and how those adducts dissociate. “Mechanism” (0.085) and “adducts” (0.080) have the highest within-community PageRank, while “pyridine” (0.060) and “platinum” (0.050) suggest a focus on metal–ligand interactions. This connects the community to Community 1’s work on the structure and reactivity of metal complexes and to Community 2’s interest in how ligands are arranged around metal centres. The emphasis here is on the steps by which those associations form or come apart. The keyword table leaves open whether the pyridine and platinum terms refer to the same set of compounds.

Alongside it, “cations,” “dications,” and “Lewis acids” point to research on bonding and electron-pair acceptance in positively charged species.
The closest overlap is with Community 1, which also examines the structure and reactivity of metal complexes. Here, the focus narrows to phosphorus compounds and the role of ligands in reactions such as palladium cross-coupling. Crystal structures and molecular calculations connect the community to Community 2’s work on determining and interpreting structure. The emphasis on binding also links it to the adduct community, where the question is how associations form and dissociate.

title: Chemistry
text:
This community in Cluster 7 examines the structure and reactivity of transition-metal complexes. “X-ray structure” has the highest within-community PageRank (0.102), followed by “asymmetric catalysis” (0.057), “tantalum” (0.054), and “oxidation” (0.052). “Metal-carbon bonds,” “niobium,” and “titanocene” give the community an organometallic focus. The catalytic terms point to two kinds of work. Asymmetric catalysis concerns reactions that favour one mirror-image form of a product, while olefin polymerization and ring-opening metathesis polymerization concern how small molecules are joined into polymer chains.
The combination of structural characterization and reactivity connects this community to Community 1’s work on metal complexes. X-ray structure also connects it to Community 2’s interest in how researchers determine molecular arrangements. Its catalytic focus differs from that of the phosphorus and Lewis acidity community, where palladium cross-coupling is the named application. Here, the keywords give more attention to controlling the spatial arrangement of reaction products and to building polymers.

The emphasis on structural characterization connects this community to Community 2’s work on crystal and molecular structure. The chemistry it foregrounds is different from that of the preceding community, where X-ray structure appears alongside transition-metal complexes, asymmetric catalysis, and polymerization. Here, the most distinctive terms concern salts and ionic liquids. “Ethylene,” “alpha-olefins,” and “aldehydes” also appear, though the keyword table leaves open how those reagents relate to the ionic liquids work.

The closest connection is to Community 2, which also uses diffraction to determine structure. Here, the emphasis is on the arrangement of molecules relative to one another and the hydrogen bonds that help hold them together. The adduct community offers another parallel through its interest in how chemical species associate. Its keywords emphasize formation and dissociation, while this community emphasizes the structures that molecular associations produce in solids.

These properties help determine whether a compound can serve as a starting material for growing a thin film.
The focus on metal complexes connects this work to Community 1, and the use of molecular structure to characterize compounds connects it to Community 2. Here, those questions serve a materials application. Researchers are interested in how the structure and thermal behaviour of a compound affect its suitability for deposition. “Hydrosilylation” also points to work on catalytic reactivity within the same grouping.

Molecular orbital calculations, conformations, and electron diffraction point to work on how molecules are arranged and how their electrons are distributed. Condensation and Diels–Alder reactions give the community a focus in organic transformations, while ruthenium, carbenes, olefin metathesis, and hydrogenation point to an organometallic strand.
The community overlaps with Community 2 in its use of calculations and diffraction to study structure, and with Community 1 in its attention to how compounds react. Its emphasis is on structure and reactivity in the context of specific transformations, from reactions that form rings to those that rearrange or reduce carbon–carbon double bonds.

Here, the ligand’s role in electron transfer is the focus.

title: Evolution
text:
Geology is the main focus of Cluster 1, accounting for seven of its ten keyword communities. These communities use the rock record to ask how landscapes, basins, and continents took shape. Several focus on Atlantic Canada at different scales. One reconstructs the geological history of the northern Appalachians and the Maritimes, while another traces where sediments in offshore basins came from and how burial, heat, and fluids changed them. The North Mountain Basalt community narrows the focus to a rock formation in Nova Scotia and its place in the history of volcanism and rifting around the Bay of Fundy.
Other geological communities connect regional histories to questions about how rocks and mineral deposits form. Research in southern Mexico uses rock ages and evidence of burial and deformation to reconstruct ancient plate boundaries. Work in northwest China combines questions about how continental crust grew with research on what basin sediments reveal about past environments. The volcanic-rock geochemistry and mineralization communities both ask what happens as magma changes. In the first, the aim is to explain the composition of volcanic rocks. In the second, it is to understand how crystallization and the movement of hot fluids concentrate elements and form deposits.
“Evolution” captures a recurring concern with origins and change over time. In astronomy, researchers model how clouds of gas collapse and how young stars gather material. That same keyword community also includes research on sexual selection and population structure. A separate community focuses on the evolutionary history and classification of grasses, using DNA and plant traits to trace relationships among lineages. These studies differ in what they examine and what counts as evidence, but each uses observations available today to explain how something came to be.
Corporate finance forms a distinct strand in the same institutional corpus. Its keywords point to how firms’ access to cash, use of debt, and internal conflicts of interest shape investment decisions and how efficiently firms allocate capital.
Three forms of evidence below show what the keyword communities are about and how they relate to one another.
Interactive keyword network. Each point represents a keyword, and a line connects two keywords that appear together in one or more publications. The full network shows how keyword communities relate to one another. Select a community from the dropdown to see which terms group together and which connect to terms in other communities. Connections within a community show which subjects, methods, or concepts appear together. Connections across communities show where their vocabularies overlap.
Community word clouds. Each cloud shows the vocabulary of one community. Larger words have higher within-community PageRank. This measure reflects both the strength of a keyword’s connections and how well connected its neighbours are. Larger words therefore show which terms are most prominent in the community’s pattern of connections. Smaller words can give those terms context by identifying particular subjects, settings, or methods.
Affiliated publications. Each publication has a set of membership values, one for each community. A value of 1 means that all of the publication’s keyword-based membership is assigned to that community. When membership is distributed across communities, the values show how that affiliation is shared. For example, values of 0.7 and 0.3 indicate that the publication’s keywords align more strongly with the first community while also connecting it to the second. The publication lists show how the themes visible in the keyword network are represented in the institution’s research.

















Community 1 of Cluster 1 centres on how stars form and evolve. “Evolution” has the highest within-community PageRank (0.141), more than five times that of “models” (0.027), the next-ranked term. “Hydrodynamics,” “stars: formation,” “collapse,” and “accretion” point to research that models how interstellar clouds collapse and how young stars gather material. Protoplanetary disks connect this work to the formation of planetary systems, while stellar oscillations point to how researchers probe the internal structure of stars.
The community also contains a strand in which evolution takes on a biological meaning. “Kinship,” “pairwise relatedness,” and “gene flow” point to research on how populations are structured. “Sexual size dimorphism,” “mating success,” and “mate preferences” point to research on sexual selection. In this community, “evolution” names two kinds of inquiry, with the highest-ranking subject terms giving the community its focus on stars.












Community 2 of Cluster 1 focuses on where magmas come from and how they change before forming volcanic rocks. “Geochemistry” has the highest within-community PageRank (0.071), followed by “volcanic rocks” (0.040) and “petrogenesis” (0.037), the study of how rocks form. Trace elements and isotopes of neodymium and strontium provide clues to a magma’s source. Terms such as “fractional crystallization,” “magma mixing,” and “crustal contamination” point to ways its composition can change as minerals crystallize, magmas mix, or magma interacts with the surrounding crust. Subduction zones, continental rifts, and mantle plumes give these questions different tectonic settings.
Like the star formation community, this community asks how the objects it studies came to be. Community 1 uses observations and models to investigate how stars form and evolve. Here, the chemical composition of rocks provides evidence about the sources and histories of the magmas that formed them.












Community 3 of Cluster 1 reconstructs the geological history of Atlantic Canada and the northern Appalachians. “Nova Scotia” has the highest within-community PageRank (0.088), followed by “New Brunswick” (0.031), “rocks” (0.031), and “Canada” (0.027). The geological terms give that regional focus more detail. “Maritimes Basin” and “clastic unit” point to work on sedimentary deposits and how basins filled. “Avalonia,” “Meguma,” and “Ganderia” point to questions about how blocks of crust with distinct geological histories came together. Uranium–lead dating and other isotope analyses help establish when events occurred and where rock or sediment came from.
The closest connection is to Community 2’s work on volcanic-rock geochemistry. Both use the chemical and isotopic record in rocks to reconstruct past events. Community 2 emphasizes where magmas came from and how they changed across tectonic settings. Community 3 uses some of the same evidence, alongside sedimentary records and rock ages, to explain how a region took shape.












Community 4 of Cluster 1 examines how plant lineages arose and how their evolutionary relationships inform classification. “Origin” has the highest within-community PageRank (0.056), followed by “Triticeae” (0.052), “classification” (0.046), and “Poaceae” (0.042). These terms place the focus within the grass family, particularly the tribe that includes wheat, barley, and Elymus. “RPB2 gene,” “chloroplast genome,” and “morphology” point to the kinds of evidence researchers compare to reconstruct ancestry. “Introgression,” “polyploidy,” and “multiple origins” suggest why those histories can be difficult to untangle: lineages can exchange genetic material through interbreeding, and similar forms can arise more than once. Arabidopsis also appears, extending the plant research beyond grasses.
This community connects most directly to the biological strand of Community 1. There, kinship and gene flow point to how populations are structured, while mating success and mate preferences point to sexual selection. Here, the emphasis is on how plant lineages arose and how to classify them. The connection to the geological communities is in the use of present-day evidence to reconstruct origins, with genes and plant traits providing a different kind of record from rock chemistry and isotopes.












Community 5 of Cluster 1 examines where sediments came from, how they accumulated, and how they changed after deposition along the eastern Canadian continental margin. “Provenance” has the highest within-community PageRank (0.062), followed by “offshore Nova Scotia” (0.036) and “margin” (0.028). The Scotian Basin and the Grand Banks give the work a regional focus. Minerals such as zircon and detrital muscovite provide clues to the source rocks, while stratigraphy helps reconstruct the sequence in which sediments accumulated. “Diagenesis,” “thermal history,” and “fluid inclusions” point to a further question about how burial, heating, and fluid movement altered the resulting rocks.
This community extends Community 3’s work on the geological history of Atlantic Canada offshore, with a more specific focus on sedimentary basins. It also shares Community 2’s interest in reconstructing origins from rocks. In the volcanic-rock community, the question is where magmas came from and how they changed. Here, it is where sediment grains came from and what those grains and the rocks they form can tell us about a basin’s history.












Community 6 of Cluster 1 examines what the rocks of southern Mexico reveal about the former positions of continents and oceans. “Geochronology” (0.054), “Acatlán Complex” (0.050), and “Mexico” (0.047) have the highest within-community PageRank. The Acatlán and Oaxacan complexes anchor the work in southern Mexico, while “Laurentia,” “Gondwana,” “Rheic Ocean,” and “Pangea” point to questions about where blocks of crust once lay and how they came together. title: The SMU-affiliated Research Corpus
text:
Introduction
The expansion of corporate management models within higher education over the past several decades has begun to change how academic knowledge is produced, evaluated, and incentivised. To greater and lesser degrees, universities have transitioned away from traditional collegial governance structures toward managerial frameworks, commonly known as New Public Management (NPM). Under this corporate paradigm, senior university administration relies on institutional strategic research plans, formal performance indicators, and centralised accountability metrics to align faculty behaviours with broader organisational objectives.
Below, I review some recent scholarship on academic managerialism to contextualise what for me, is becoming an increasinly intersting question: do strategic research plans work?

title: The SMU-affiliated Research Corpus
text:
Academic Managerialism
The introduction of corporate steering in public research sectors is frequently framed as a necessary mechanism to increase operational efficiency and institutional accountability. Scholars examining the Central and Eastern European contexts demonstrate that department heads are forced to act as primary mediators, negotiating the friction between emerging corporate managerial expectations and traditional academic autonomy (Machovcova, Zabrodska, and Mudrak 2019). This transition shifts the university from an open site of unconstrained intellectual inquiry to a managed environment where output is being both quantified and regularised. Empirical observations of these policy shifts suggest that while they aim to stimulate public research efficiency, they can function as a double-edged sword, leading to administrative inflation and narrow publishing strategies among faculty (Schubert 2009).
The global reach of these corporate practices is evident across diverse higher education landscapes, including developing regions such as the United Arab Emirates, where new managerialism is deployed to reshape institutional reputations (Ajayan and Balasubramanian 2020). When fiscal cutbacks occur, the pressure to maintain research performance becomes even more acute; institutions are forced to sustain or accelerate output levels even when financial incentives and direct support is declines (Bak and Kim 2023). At the core of this management system is the corporate premise that academic institutions are structurally no different from any commercial enterprise and can therefore be optimised through auditing and performance-monitoring systems (Hasham 2018). Consequently, the historical evolution of research performance measurement systems, particularly within heavily evaluated sectors like Australian higher education, outlines a steady intensification of administrative oversight (Martin-Sardesai et al. 2019).

title: The SMU-affiliated Research Corpus
section: Institutional Leadership and Strategic Shared Visions
text:
Institutional Leadership and Strategic Shared Visions
A central tenet of corporate strategic planning is that institutional leadership is in a position to steer research excellence. Recent quantitative modeling of presidential capabilities in Chinese higher education argues that specific strategic competencies at the executive level correlate positively with institutional performance gains and international visibility (Dong, Wu, and Yu 2025). Similarly, evaluations of academic leadership and university performance across European and Russian contexts investigate whether universities demonstrate measurable improvements when led by active, highly cited scholars who embody research excellence, rather than pure career administrators (Gerashchenko 2022). This structural steering is frequently reinforced by regional contagion effects, where the strategic choices and performance trajectories of neighbouring peer institutions create a normative pressure that drives local academic leadership to adopt identical strategic management models (Saftiuc, Proscanu, and Teodorescu 2025).
For these administrative plans to translate into scholarly output, university leaders direct attention to building an institutional shared vision that attempts to bridge the historical divide between research and teaching mandates (Bui et al. 2024). Senior management relies on transformational leadership styles, operating under the assumption that inspiring a collective corporate identity will foster internal creativity and outputs (Salim and Zakaria 2021). In fields such as green innovation and technology transfer, evidence indicates that the specific academic and corporate experiences of the top management team can shape the volume and direction of institutional innovation outputs (Zhao et al. 2021). Moreover, when academic executives retain active boardroom connections, they can connect lab-based research with high-impact industrial commercialisation, demonstrating how top-down strategies attempt to steer basic science toward applied economic utility (Zhu, Wu, and Gaidai 2025).

title: The SMU-affiliated Research Corpus
text:
Guiding Research Productivity
At the level of the faculty member, the primary mechanisms used to enforce strategic alignment are institutional incentives, formal performance appraisals, and individual research productivity tracking. Evidence suggests that while structured interventions can alter short-term output counts, they rarely change long-term scholarly trajectories (Ryazanova and Jaskiene 2022). While routine bibliometric reports are frequently positioned as one tool among many, these data summaries often function as coercive monitoring mechanisms that hold individual faculty accountable to generic performance targets (Cabezas-Clavijo and Torres-Salinas 2021). In some cases, advanced institutional frameworks have emerged, such as bibliometric strength, potential, and risk analysis models, which allow administrators to track exactly how faculty publication choices respond to central strategic choices and funding pathways (Iping et al. 2024).
The efficacy of these incentive structures remains dependent on localized professional contexts and personal scholarly investments. In Canada, broad empirical studies of primary care researchers demonstrate that productivity is strongly associated with protected research time, dedicated infrastructure, and targeted team-based funding rather than purely top-down corporate mandates (Aggarwal et al. 2024). Furthermore, the specialized nature of research production is heavily reliant on specific cognitive resources and long-term personal investments, which means that arbitrary administrative redirections can result in cognitive friction and operational inefficiency for the scholar (Degli Antoni, Fia, and Sacconi 2022). Quantitative analyses of individual academic research agendas confirm that broader organizational factors and institutional priorities interact directly with disciplinary traditions, meaning that top-down steering tools must constantly compete with an academic’s internalized scholarly values and peer networks (Horta and Santos 2020).

title: The SMU-affiliated Research Corpus
text:
Tensions, Resistance, and Academic Freedom
The imposition of corporate performance management has generated tensions, with many scholars arguing that these frameworks stifle academic freedom and distort genuine knowledge production. Critical discourse analyses highlight that aggressive performance management frameworks force a precarious state of affairs upon academic work, transforming scholarly writing into a rushed commodity designed to satisfy auditing cycles rather than solve profound intellectual problems (Morrish and Sauntson 2016). This shift creates a sense of alienation, where academic identities are systematically reconfigured to fit the parameters of the managed university, sparking widespread subtle resistance among faculty who seek to protect their professional autonomy from neoliberal encroachment (Morrish 2017). In specialized fields like social work education, the imposition of a marketized, neo-liberal agenda is shown to directly compromise the critical, social-justice mission of the discipline by prioritizing commercial metric capture over community engagement (MacDonald and Nixon 2016).
The human cost of these auditing regimes is captured in qualitative terms by academics who describe the modern pressure cooker environment (Xu and Poole 2024). This creates institutional struggles for recognition where individual departments are pitted against one another for scarce resources, fragmenting the university’s traditional community of scholars (Muench and Baier 2012). Moreover, the formal policies and administrative structures often lack meaningful faculty buy-in because they are perceived as top-down compliance exercises rather than authentic scholarly transformations (Castro-Gomez et al. 2026). Without aligning internal policy incentives directly with the intrinsic motivations and professional values of the faculty, centralized administrative mandates fail to cultivate genuine participation or sustainable scholarly growth (Barsallo et al. 2026).

title: The SMU-affiliated Research Corpus
text:
Do Strategic Research Plans Work?
This breief review on higher education management demonstrates a conflict between top-down corporate steering and bottom-up faculty behaviour. While institutional theories and administrative models posit that clear leadership capabilities, shared corporate visions, and targeted bibliometric monitoring can successfully optimize and direct an institution’s research performance, empirical accounts expose resistance, strategic gaming, and profound alignment failures. This contradiction exposes a gap in evaluative scientometrics: we lack robust, objective, longitudinal measures of whether corporate university strategies genuinely shape the intellectual landscape of an institution or if they merely retroactively rebrand pre-existing, faculty-driven strengths.
It is with this in mind that I raise the following question: do strategic research plans work?
I explore this question turning to the research corpus of Saint Mary’s University (SMU).

title: The SMU-affiliated Research Corpus
text:
Data
This bibliometric study examines 36 years of SMU-affiliated research, from January 1990 through December 2025. The corpus is restricted to publications for which the institutional affiliation metadata explicitly identifies SMU. No restrictions were placed on document type. These deliberately broad parameters were intended to capture the full range of scholarly outputs indexed by Web of Science (WoS) that can be attributed to faculty, staff, and researchers associated with SMU, providing a basis for examining publication behaviour, research activity, and patterns of connection and collaboration across the university community over the period.
The search produced a corpus of 7,850 publications appearing across 2,862 different publication sources, reflecting a wide range of scholarly venues and the disciplinary breadth of the university. The corpus should not, however, be treated as a complete inventory of everything produced at SMU. Web of Science is widely used for bibliometric research, but, like all bibliographic databases, it is selective. Its coverage tends to favour English-language journals and disciplines in which journal articles and collaborative publication are dominant forms of scholarly communication. Fields in which research is more often communicated through books, book chapters, regional journals, professional publications, or other locally oriented venues may therefore be less completely represented. This is particularly consequential for some areas of the humanities and social sciences. The analysis should accordingly be understood as a description of the SMU research activity visible through Web of Science rather than an exhaustive account of the university’s entire research culture.

title: Work, governance, and well-being
text:
Cluster 2 brings together research on work, governance, and well-being. Two communities examine different stages of working life. Personnel selection research asks how employers assess applicants, how applicants manage the impressions they make, and whether interview ratings predict job performance. The workplace stress and leadership community examines how supervision, job demands, and social support relate to burnout, safety, job satisfaction, and turnover.
The corporate governance community examines who oversees firms, what firms disclose, and how investors assess their performance. The gender and inequality community looks at organizations and labour markets from the perspective of who gains access to work and how earnings and opportunities vary across social groups. Its research on identity, religion, and belonging extends that inquiry beyond employment. Environmental governance takes questions about authority and participation into another setting. Here, the focus is on how institutions and communities share decisions about resources, protect ecosystems, and respond to climate risks that can affect livelihoods unevenly.
The physical activity community shares the workplace community’s interest in health and the conditions that shape it. It examines how common physical activity is, how it fits into adults’ daily routines, and what limits participation. Work on classifying activities and measuring how people spend their time helps researchers compare activity patterns across populations.
Three forms of evidence below show what the keyword communities are about and how they relate to one another.
Interactive keyword network. Each point represents a keyword, and a line connects two keywords that appear together in one or more publications. The full network shows how keyword communities relate to one another. Select a community from the dropdown to see which terms group together and which connect to terms in other communities. Connections within a community show which subjects, methods, or concepts appear together. Connections across communities show where their vocabularies overlap.
Community word clouds. Each cloud shows the vocabulary of one community. Larger words have higher within-community PageRank. This measure reflects both the strength of a keyword’s connections and how well connected its neighbours are. Larger words therefore show which terms are most prominent in the community’s pattern of connections. Smaller words can give those terms context by identifying particular subjects, settings, or methods.
Affiliated publications. Each publication has a set of membership values, one for each community. A value of 1 means that all of the publication’s keyword-based membership is assigned to that community. When membership is distributed across communities, the values show how that affiliation is shared. For example, values of 0.7 and 0.3 indicate that the publication’s keywords align more strongly with the first community while also connecting it to the second. The publication lists show how the themes visible in the keyword network are represented in the institution’s research.

















Community 1 of Cluster 2 brings together research on how working conditions and relationships shape employee behaviour, health, and well-being. One strand concerns leadership and supervision. Its vocabulary ranges from transformational leadership and social support to abusive supervision, incivility, and workplace aggression. title: Co-word Analysis
text:
I use keyword co-occurrence analysis to examine the substantive organization of the SMU-affiliated corpus. The method belongs to the same broad family of bibliometric techniques as co-citation and co-author analysis, but its object is different: rather than asking which authors collaborate or which publications are cited together, it asks which research keywords co-occur across a collection of publications. Authors and databases use keywords to characterize the content of a publication, typically identifying concepts, topics, methods, populations, objects of study, or research problems. The underlying assumption is that these keywords are not distributed randomly. When two keywords repeatedly appear together in the same publications, that recurrence provides evidence that the ideas are being brought into relation within the literature. Co-word analysis therefore allows me to move from a collection of individual publications to a representation of the substantive relationships that recur across the corpus, without beginning from a predetermined classification of the literature.
A keyword co-occurrence network is constructed by first counting these relationships. In the simplified example, a co-occurrence matrix contains six research keywords in its rows and columns, with each intersecting cell recording how many times a pair of keywords appears together. Sport and Identity, for example, have a co-occurrence value of five, whereas Identity and Network Analysis co-occur only once.

The matrix is then converted into an undirected, weighted network using methods of network analysis. Each keyword becomes a node, and an edge connects two nodes when the corresponding keywords occur together in at least one publication. The weight of the edge records the frequency of that co-occurrence, allowing more recurrent relationships to be represented by thicker lines.
Once represented as a network, additional measures can be used to describe the position of individual keywords and the structure of the network as a whole. Degree records the number of other keywords to which a keyword is directly connected, so a high-degree keyword is more extensively embedded in the network than one with relatively few connections. Clustering algorithms such as Louvain identify groups of keywords that are more densely connected to one another than to the rest of the network.
Example Keyword Co-Occurrence Network
In the toy example, Masculinity, Sport, and Identity form one such group, while Network Analysis, Bibliometrics, and Data Science form another. The strongest relationships include Network Analysis–Bibliometrics (6), Sport–Identity (5), and Bibliometrics–Data Science (5). By contrast, the single co-occurrence between Identity and Network Analysis creates a comparatively weak bridge between the two clusters. The visualization therefore makes both internal cohesion and cross-cluster connection visible. Spatial position should be interpreted cautiously, however, because it is partly a consequence of the layout algorithm rather than an independent substantive property.
What the resulting network reveals is not simply which keywords are common, but how the substantive vocabulary of a research corpus is organized relationally. Nodes identify the concepts present in the literature; degree indicates how broadly those concepts are connected; edge weights show which associations recur more or less frequently; and clusters identify concentrations of keywords that repeatedly occur together. When the highly connected keywords within a cluster point toward a coherent substantive concern, those clusters can reasonably be interpreted as research areas or thematic formations. The network can also identify bridging concepts that connect otherwise distinct areas of research and more peripheral keywords that occupy specialized positions.

title: Co-word Analysis
text:
The SMU-affiliated keyword network
In what follows, I use keyword co-occurrence analysis to map recurring intellectual associations within the SMU-affiliated corpus of 7,850 publications. The network focuses on how the keywords used to describe those publications are connected. Groups of densely connected keywords are represented as clusters, but these clusters should not be understood as predetermined departments, disciplines, or administrative categories. They are emergent groupings of concepts, research problems, methods, populations, and objects of study that recur together across the corpus. The resulting network therefore provides a way of examining both what SMU-affiliated researchers study and how different areas of research are related within the indexed literature.
A connection between two keywords indicates that the keywords have been used together in describing the same scholarly output; it does not imply that they have the same meaning or necessarily belong to the same discipline. What matters analytically is the pattern of relationships among keywords. A keyword may be highly connected because it appears alongside many different topics, while another may occupy a more specialized position because its connections are concentrated within a narrower area of research. The network is therefore best understood as a map of research association and connectedness rather than simply a count of topics.
The network combines two forms of keyword metadata. Author keywords are keywords selected by authors to describe the subject matter of their publications, while database-generated keywords, such as Keywords Plus, are derived from information in the bibliographic record to identify additional topical relationships. These were combined before constructing the network to provide a broader representation of the subjects and concepts associated with each publication. As a result, a node labelled migration, galaxies, or education represents a keyword in the bibliographic description of the corpus, not a researcher, department, publication, or project.
The vocabulary itself is heterogeneous. Some keywords identify broad substantive areas, while others refer to theoretical concepts, research methods, populations, geographic locations, objects of study, scientific processes, or highly specialized phenomena. Because author-supplied and database-generated keywords are combined, the network should be interpreted as a representation of how SMU research is bibliographically described and connected, rather than as a direct inventory of the concepts researchers themselves would necessarily identify as most important.

How to use the network and tables
The interactive network provides the broadest view of these relationships. Use the keyword search above the network to locate a particular keyword. Selecting a keyword highlights its node in yellow with a black border. Once selected, the nodes connected directly to that keyword are also highlighted. The network can then be zoomed and panned to bring these linked nodes into focus, and individual nodes may be dragged to make crowded areas easier to inspect. Moving a node changes only its position on the screen and does not alter the underlying network analysis.
When you look at a keyword together with all of its neighbours, you are looking at that keyword’s immediate local network. The selected keyword is the focal keyword, and each neighbour is another keyword that appeared with it in the metadata of at least one publication in the corpus. The neighbourhood therefore shows the set of topics, concepts, methods, populations, places, or objects of study that have been directly associated with that keyword in SMU-affiliated research. This neighbourhood can be interpreted as a picture of the keyword’s intellectual context. A keyword with neighbours drawn largely from its own cluster is embedded mainly within a relatively concentrated area of research. Selecting the keywords “behaviour”, “radial velocities”, “health”, “management history”, or “actor network theory” from the keyword drop down search menu offers an illustration of this type of pattern. A keyword whose neighbours span several clusters may instead connect otherwise distinct areas of scholarly activity. Selecting the keywords “origin”, “sequence”, or “evolution” will illustrate this type of pattern.
Nodes with the same colour belong to the same intellectual cluster.1 Node size represents degree of connectedness: larger nodes are directly connected to a greater number of other keywords in the network, while smaller nodes have fewer direct connections and tend to occupy more specialized positions. Node size therefore represents network connectedness rather than the quality, importance, or volume of research associated with a keyword.
The tables provide complementary ways of examining the same network.

The Keyword neighbours table allows a reader to select an exact keyword and retrieve all of the keywords directly connected to it, ordered by the strength of their co-occurrence. This value is a measure of how often the focal keyword and a particular neighbour appear together in the publication metadata. For example, searching for the keyword “health” in this table reveals that “health” and “canada” co-occur 9 times in this dataset.
The Cluster profiles table provides a compact overview of the vocabulary associated with each intellectual cluster.
The Cluster vocabulary table lists every keyword in the network by cluster, allowing readers to move beyond the most prominent keywords and examine more specialized areas that may be difficult to identify visually.
The Author lookup table will return the titles of publications of an author. This presented partly as a means of allowing those interested to think through and assess the coverage of the WoS database.

The Cluster profiles and Cluster vocabulary look up tables provide insight into the structure of these clusters. The tables report each keyword’s rank and degree.2

If you’ve made it this far…
On this basis of the above, what begins to emerge is that the SMU-affiliated research corpus contains 7 research clusters whose “identities” have yet to be specified.
In the same way that the all the keywords used in the SMU-affiliated corpus can be arranged in a network and “decomposed” into 7 clusters, each of these 7 clusters can be explored in the same way. “Decomposing” these research clusters allows for their structure to be explored more carefully, opening up an opportunity to think more clearly about what each of these 7 research clusters is “about”–and what this might say about the university as a whole.
At the top of the page, you’ll find links to details about each of the 7 research clusters. Currently, only data for Clusters 1 and 7 are available. In the spirit of “member checking” (Birt et al. 2016; McKim 2023), I invite you to review these details. Does this data resonate with your understanding of your own scholarly activity and/or the activity at SMU?
